# Differences from the originals

Where BlitzLLVM can not behave like Blitz3D or BlitzPlus, because the system they were made for is gone, this is how it behaves instead.

## Multiplayer

The multiplayer commands (`StartNetGame`, `HostNetGame`, `JoinNetGame`, `StopNetGame`, `CreateNetPlayer`, `DeleteNetPlayer`, `SendNetMsg`, `RecvNetMsg` and the rest) used DirectPlay in the originals, which is no longer available. In BlitzLLVM the programs that join a game connect to the program that hosts it over TCP, on port 40500. The host passes messages on to the other programs.

* Games made with BlitzLLVM can only play with other games made with BlitzLLVM. They can not join, or be joined by, a program made with Blitz3D.
* The port can be changed with the environment variable `BLITZ_NETGAME_PORT`. Every program of a game has to use the same one, and the host needs it to be open in its firewall.
* `StartNetGame` shows a dialog that asks whether to host or to join. When joining, the address of the host is asked on the console.
* The environment variable `BLITZ_DIALOG_ANSWER` presses a button of a dialog without showing it (0 is the first button), which is meant for automated runs.

## Network addresses

`CountHostIPs` looks up a host and remembers its addresses for `HostIP`. An empty name is this computer, which has one address for every network interface that is up, with the loopback address (127.0.0.1) last. `UDPStreamIP` is the first of those. Only IPv4 addresses are returned.

## Mip maps

Textures with flag 8 get a chain of mip maps and are sampled with trilinear filtering, which blends between two levels. The levels are made by averaging 2 by 2 texels, so masked (flag 4) and alpha textures average their alpha as well, which is also what the original did and makes their edges soft from afar. The levels of a texture that is drawn on (`TextureBuffer`) are made again before the texture is next used in a scene. The levels that are stored in a block compressed DDS file are used instead of made ones. A texture with frames (`LoadAnimTexture`, `CreateTexture` with frames) is one sheet, so its smallest levels blend the frames that are next to each other. There is no anisotropic filtering.

## Depth buffer

The depth buffer is reversed and a 32-bit float: the near plane of `CameraRange` is written as 1 and the far plane as 0, and the closer surface wins. Blitz3D used a 16 or 24-bit buffer that is 0 at the near plane, which spends most of its precision close to the camera and makes far surfaces flicker through each other (z-fighting). With the reversed float buffer the precision is almost even over the whole range, so distant surfaces that are close together stay apart without having to push `near` out. This changes nothing a program can see except that z-fighting is much rarer. The depth is still not linear in the buffer itself (it is `near / distance` for a perspective camera, and linear for `CameraProjMode 2`), but the buffer is never read back by a program: `ProjectedZ` is the distance in front of the camera, and `Graphics3D`'s depth argument is not used.

## Console window on Windows

Programs are built for the GUI subsystem, so starting one (by double click, or from a window of the program) does not open a console window next to its own window. If the program is started from a terminal, it uses that terminal: `Print`, `Write`, `Input`, `DebugLog` and runtime errors work as on other systems, and they follow the redirection of the terminal (`program.exe > out.txt` writes `Print` to the file, `2> log.txt` writes `DebugLog`). Started without a terminal there is nothing to print to, so `Print` and `DebugLog` show nothing (`DebugLog` still goes to an attached debugger), and a runtime error is shown in a message box. The terminal does not wait for a GUI program, so its prompt may appear before the output of the program ends; use `start /wait program.exe` to wait. A program that runs `blitzcc` without `-o` runs from `blitzcc`'s terminal, so its output is shown as usual.

For a program that never opens a window, build it with `blitzcc --console`, which creates a console program that opens a console window when started without a terminal. This is only done for Windows, other systems always have the console they were started from.

## Stop

`Stop` is a breakpoint for a debugger. In a debug build (`-d`) it is a breakpoint instruction (`llvm.debugtrap`), which stops in an attached debugger and ends the program with a signal when there is none. In any other build it does nothing.

## AppTitle

The second argument of `AppTitle` is asked when somebody closes the window. If they cancel, the program carries on; otherwise the window closes as it would have without the question.

## SystemProperty

| Property | Windows | Elsewhere |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `appdir` | The folder of the program. | The folder of the program. |
| `tempdir` | `%TEMP%` | `$TEMP`, `$TMPDIR` or `/tmp`. |
| `windowsdir` | `%SystemRoot%` | `/etc/` (`/System/` on macOS), where the system keeps its settings. |
| `systemdir` | The System32 folder. | `/usr/lib/` (`/System/Library/` on macOS), where the system keeps its libraries. |

Folders end with a separator, except for the ones of Windows, which are as the system gives them.

## Colors

The 3D commands that take a color (`EntityColor`, `BrushColor`, `VertexColor`, `LightColor`, `AmbientLight`, `CameraClsColor`, `CameraFogColor`, `BSPAmbientLight` and the color of `LightMesh`) take floats from 0 to 255, so programs that pass whole numbers work as before. Vertex colors are stored as 16-bit floats (also on the GPU) and not as one byte per part, so `VertexColor` followed by `VertexRed`, `VertexGreen`, `VertexBlue` and `VertexAlpha` returns what was set (limited to 0 to 255, and 0 to 1 for alpha) to within about 0.1 of the 0 to 255 scale and `LightMesh` adds light without rounding the colors in between. The 2D commands (`Color`, `ClsColor`, `GetColor` and `ColorRed`, `ColorGreen`, `ColorBlue`) work on pixels and stay whole numbers.

## Sound resampling

The original played sounds through FMOD, which brings them to the rate of the sound device with linear interpolation. That leaves mirror images of the sound above its own bandwidth, which makes sounds with a low rate (11025 Hz files like the rain of Stranded II) bright and crisp, and takes a little off the top of the rest. SDL_mixer resamples cleanly, so the same files sound duller. Set the environment variable `BLITZ_AUDIO_CLASSIC` (to anything) before the program starts to do what the original did. Pitch and looping are the same either way.
